implementation_notes: threading.Lock, RLock, Semaphore and Condition implement the context-manager protocol, so `with lock:` is the complete realization: __enter__ acquires, __exit__ releases even when the body raises, and the with-block is the critical section. For asyncio, asyncio.Lock is an async context manager (`async with lock:`), which suspends the task instead of blocking the loop. The with-statement replaces both the POSA2 guard class and any try/finally, and contextlib.ExitStack can hold a dynamically determined set of locks with the same guarantee.
code_sketch:
import threading

counts: dict[str, int] = {}
lock = threading.Lock()

def increment(key: str) -> None:
    with lock:                             # acquire on entry
        counts[key] = counts.get(key, 0) + 1   # critical section
    # __exit__ released the lock on every path, including exceptions
pitfalls: threading.Lock is not reentrant: a nested `with lock:` in the same thread deadlocks; RLock only if the re-entrancy is genuinely by design.
The GIL does not make read-modify-write atomic - counts[k] += 1, setdefault sequences and check-then-act still need the lock (and free-threaded builds remove even the appearance of safety).
asyncio.Lock requires `async with`; using `with` raises (no __enter__), and holding it across CPU-bound work blocks the loop because the task never awaits.
Locks created at import time can bind to the wrong loop or be shared between processes after fork; create asyncio primitives inside the running loop and re-create locks after fork.
